fields.title: Failover as a Product Event
fields.keyTakeaway: Failover breaks operations, loses unreplicated data, and hits cold caches, so it must be practiced under load, and its product consequences must be designed in advance.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: The region is down, switching to backup. What happens to the user?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Failover is neither instantaneous nor free, and its product consequences include lost data, broken sessions, and repeated actions. If not designed in advance, they turn a controlled event into a second-order incident.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: *Interruption of current operations.* Everything running gets cut off. Users get errors. *Loss of unreplicated data.* With asynchronous replication, data from the last seconds or minutes has not arrived — this is the actual RPO of the failover. *Broken sessions.* If sessions are stored locally, everyone gets logged out. *Cold caches.* The backup region runs slowly for the first few minutes until caches warm up. Under full load, this can crash it. *External webhooks.* Providers keep sending to the old address until DNS updates.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: The last two are why unverified failovers usually fail: the backup site either cannot handle full load or misses incoming events.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: Hence the practice: **failover is tested regularly through drills under real load.** Some companies keep the backup region running on a fraction of traffic precisely for this reason.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: [[failback|Failback]] is a separate operation, often more complex than failover: while the backup ran, data accumulated that needs to be brought back.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: Product decisions made in advance: what to show during failover, whether users get logged out, what to do with broken operations, whom to notify.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Inter-zone failover is automatic, taking about two minutes. Product behavior: the app shows "restoring connection" and retries requests with jitter — without jitter, all clients hit the database simultaneously and finish off the newly revived database.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: Sessions are moved to a shared storage accessible from all zones — otherwise, every failover would log everyone out.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Quarterly failover drill at 6 AM on Sunday. The first one found three problems: caches were cold and the database could not handle the load, provider webhooks went nowhere for 4 minutes, and the order queue had a single handler instance tied to a zone — that same finding from `SC1-N3-L1`.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: It took three drills for failover to become predictable.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Automatic failover can trigger falsely and switch to backup when there is no real issue. The trigger threshold requires tuning, and failover itself is a separate metric.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Failover breaks operations, loses unreplicated data, and hits cold caches, so it must be practiced under load, and its product consequences must be designed in advance.
